title: Divisibility By Three OQ-02: Alternating Block Sums, Repunits, and Palindromes
description: An advanced extension of divisibility rules focusing on alternating k-digit block sums and their applications. Proves a general framework: when B ≡ -1 (mod d), divisibility by d is equivalent to divisibility of the alternating sum of B-ary digits of n. Applies this to divisibility by 7, 11, 13, and 1001 via alternating three-digit groups (since 1000 ≡ -1 mod 7, 11, 13, 1001). Formalizes the repunit R(k) = 111...1 (k ones), proves R(k) = (10^k - 1)/9, and provides concrete verifications of repunit divisibility and the order of 10 modulo 7, 11, 13. Proves that even-length palindromes are always divisible by 11, with explicit proofs for 2-, 4-, and 6-digit palindromes. Develops a one-step digit sum reduction theory and proves equivalence of multiple divisibility tests for 7.

meta.author: Lean Genius
originalContributions: General alternating block sum framework: alternatingSum, altBlockSum, ofDigits_modEq_alternatingSum, modEq_alternatingSum, and dvd_iff_altSum theorems
Divisibility by 7, 11, 13, and 1001 via alternating three-digit groups (1000 ≡ -1 mod each)
Nat version seven_dvd_alt_blocks_nat bridging Int and Nat divisibility for the alternating block result
Repunit definition, repunit_formula (9 × R(k) = 10^k - 1), and repunit_dvd_iff_pow_mod
Extensive concrete repunit verifications: order of 10 mod 7 is 6, mod 11 is 2, mod 13 is 6
Even-length palindrome divisibility: 2-, 4-, 6-digit palindromes are always divisible by 11
Digit sum iteration theory: digitSumStep preserves mod 9 and mod 3, is strictly decreasing for n ≥ 10
Multiple equivalent divisibility tests for 7 (base 8, base 50, base 1000 alternating)

overview.historicalContext: The observation that 1001 = 7 × 11 × 13 has long been used as a mnemonic for divisibility rules: since 1000 ≡ -1 modulo each of 7, 11, and 13, all three divisors can be tested by the same alternating three-digit block technique. Repunits (numbers consisting of all 1s) have been studied since the 19th century; their divisibility properties are related to the multiplicative order of 10 modulo various primes. The palindrome divisibility result (even-length palindromes are divisible by 11) is a delightful consequence of the alternating digit sum rule for 11.
overview.problemStatement: Prove: (1) a general alternating block sum theorem for divisibility modulo d whenever the block base B ≡ -1 (mod d); (2) specialized theorems for d ∈ {7, 11, 13, 1001} using blocks of size 3; (3) the repunit formula 9·R(k) = 10^k - 1 and the equivalence R(k) ≡ 0 (mod d) ↔ 10^k ≡ 1 (mod d) (when gcd(d,9)=1); (4) even-length palindromes are divisible by 11; (5) the digit sum step function preserves residues mod 9 and mod 3, and is strictly decreasing for n ≥ 10.
overview.proofStrategy: The general dvd_iff_altSum theorem is proved by induction on the digit list: the base case is trivial, and the inductive case uses alternatingSum_cons to rewrite and Int.ModEq.add/mul to propagate the congruence. Repunit formula by induction: 9·R(k+1) = 9·(10·R(k)+1) = 9·10·R(k) + 9 = 10·(10^k - 1) + 9 = 10^{k+1} - 1. Palindrome divisibility by direct algebraic factoring: abba = 11·(91a + 10b), etc. The digit sum step strictly decreases by Nat.sum_digits_lt.
keyInsights: The factorization 1001 = 7 × 11 × 13 means that divisibility by any of these three primes can be simultaneously tested via the same alternating three-digit block procedure
The repunit dvd criterion repunit_dvd_iff_pow_mod shows R(k) ≡ 0 (mod d) iff 10^k ≡ 1 (mod d), connecting repunit divisibility to the multiplicative order of 10
The order of 10 mod 7 is 6, mod 11 is 2, mod 13 is 6 — all verified computationally — explaining why R(6) is divisible by 7, 11, and 13 simultaneously
Even-length palindromes are always divisible by 11 because their alternating digit sum is exactly 0 by symmetry: each pair (d_i, d_{n-1-i}) contributes ±d_i - (±d_i) = 0
The digit sum step's strict decrease for n ≥ 10 (Nat.sum_digits_lt) guarantees the digital root iteration terminates — a key fact for the correctness of all digit-summing algorithms
prerequisites: Alternating digit sum framework from DivisibilityRules
Nat.sum_digits_lt for the digit sum decrease lemma

conclusion.summary: This 432-line, 31-theorem formalization develops advanced divisibility theory: the alternating block sum framework, repunit theory, even-length palindrome divisibility, and digit sum iteration. The connection between 1001 = 7 × 11 × 13 and the shared alternating three-digit block test is a highlight, formally proved and verified with concrete examples.
conclusion.implications: The general dvd_iff_altSum theorem shows that the alternating digit sum rule is not special to base 10 and modulus 11, but a universal consequence of any base-modulus pair satisfying B ≡ -1 (mod d). The repunit theory connects number theory (orders of elements in (Z/dZ)^*) to elementary digit-based reasoning. The palindrome result illustrates how formal symmetry arguments can yield clean divisibility proofs.
openQuestions: Formalize the full repunit theorem: d | R(k) iff ord_d(10) | k, for all d coprime to 10 (not just coprime to 9)
Prove that if an odd-length palindrome is divisible by 11, the middle digit must be 0 mod 11
Extend the multiple-test equivalence for 7 to a general theorem: all divisibility tests for d (digit sum in any base B ≡ 1 mod d, alternating sum in any B ≡ -1 mod d, truncation) are equivalent
